title: Instagram wants to charge you for AI photo-editing tools with Meta One
excerpt: I'll admit it: Instagram's AI photo editing tools are good. I caved and signed up for a trial of the new Meta One subscriptions.
content_html:
Instagram wants you to pay for its AI photo-editing filters — and it doesn't stop there

By Sydney Bradley

You're currently following this author! Want to unfollow? Unsubscribe via the link in your email.

I was having some unfettered fun playing with Instagram's new filters.

Then I got hit with a paywall.

"Upgrade to Meta One Core to apply more AI effects or wait until tomorrow," a pop-up said on my screen. Curious, I clicked "Upgrade."

I was given the option for a free trial of Meta One, a new subscription that unlocks a litany of perks. This week, Meta is widely rolling out its latest subscription program after announcing the plans in May.

If I accepted the monthlong trial, I could edit more photos on the app using Meta's AI "effects" it rolled out in July.

After dozens of edits tweaking my latest professional headshots to look like they were taken on a disposable camera, or turning iPhone cat photos into higher-quality editorial shots, I wanted more.

Meta has a good incentive to paywall premium features like AI.

Making people pay for more editing tools, like the Effects Instagram promotes in-app, further pushes Meta up against photo-editing rivals like Adobe's Photoshop, VSCO, and emerging apps like the influencer-founded startup Tezza.

Filters have always been part of the Instagram experience. It's why I first joined the app back in 2010. Would I have paid for photo-editing tools back then? No.

If I'm honest, though, some of Meta's new AI photo editing tools are pretty darn good. And if there weren't the threat of content being labeled as "Made with AI" on Instagram, maybe I'd even post them.

Meta is betting on subscriptions and bundles

I swiftly signed up for the Meta One Core tier — a bundle targeting everyday consumers on Meta platforms — which would renew at $7.99 a month.

The perks range from additional AI usage to unlocking the "plus" versions of Facebook, Instagram, and WhatsApp. Meta One subscribers can "preview" people's stories without actually watching them, use special app icons (like the retro Instagram one), and visually customize Facebook and WhatsApp.

There are also tiers for professional accounts (ranging from $14.99 to $499 a month). For content creators, these subscriptions unlock features like adding links to Instagram captions, getting verified, and receiving extra protection if an account is impersonated.

"For those people that want to do more, Meta One is our answer," Helen Ma, a Meta VP and head of subscriptions, said at an event on Monday, previewing the programs. "It gives subscribers more ability to do self-expression and to use more AI across our family of apps."

This isn't Meta's first attempt to get consumers to pay for a recurring subscription. In 2023, it launched Meta Verified, which charged users a monthly fee to unlock perks like a blue check mark.

It also rolled out a subscription in Europe that provides users with an ad-free experience across its apps. (It's worth noting that Ma said Meta doesn't plan on adding this perk to Meta One.)

Meta has also leaned heavily on subscriptions for its latest AI products, such as its personal assistant app Muse. It's free to start, but users will hit a cap on how much AI compute they can get from Muse — they'll either have to pay ($20 to $100 a month) or wait another day for credits to replenish.

It's similar to the paywall I hit while playing with Instagram's AI filters before being prompted to pay for Meta One.

As Meta rolls out the One subscription, Ma said the company will explore ways to give users more information about how much AI use they have left before needing to pay up.
